blocks.text: Topic A: Complex numbers

[Week 1 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/1cbac07a-cd02-48c2-8c30-c9829c4e06b2#079a564f-840a-46b1-9f12-5d8d123edad9) [Week 1 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/1cbac07a-cd02-48c2-8c30-c9829c4e06b2#fef2e73f-cd85-498c-9b6a-1ff1e058d7d3)
Complex numbers show up twice on the midterm:

items: as their own question (convert, divide, raise to a power, take roots);
inside [B5](#b5), when a characteristic equation has no real roots and you need $\sqrt{-36}=j6$.

blocks.text: **One number, two ways to write it.** A complex number is a point (an arrow) in the plane. You can give its coordinates, or its length and angle:

items: $a=\mathrm{Re}\{z\}$: the **real part**, how far right
$b=\mathrm{Im}\{z\}$: the **imaginary part**, how far up
$c=|z|$: the **magnitude**, the length of the arrow
$\theta=\angle z$: the **angle**, measured from the positive real axis
$j=\sqrt{-1}$, so $j^2=-1$ (this course writes $j$, not $i$)

blocks.text: **Converting between the two forms:**

**The quadrant trap.** The calculator’s $\tan^{-1}$ only returns angles between $-90^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. Look at the signs of $a$ and $b$ first. If $a<0$ (left half of the plane), **add $180^\circ$** to what the calculator gives.
**Arithmetic: pick the form that makes the operation easy.**

rows: add (subtract) real parts and imaginary parts separately
multiply top and bottom by the **conjugate** of the bottom: $(a+jb)^*=a-jb$

blocks.text: The conjugate works because $(a+jb)(a-jb)=a^2+b^2$, a real number. Powers of $j$ repeat every four: $j^2=-1$, $j^3=-j$, $j^4=1$, and $\dfrac1j=-j$.
**Roots: a $k$-th root question always has $k$ answers.** Write $z$ in polar form, then:

items: all $k$ roots have the **same magnitude** $c^{1/k}$;
the first is at angle $\theta/k$;
the rest follow, each $360^\circ/k$ further round the circle.

Euler’s identity $e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta$ connects the two forms. The lecture uses it to get trig identities for free: expand $e^{jA}e^{jB}=e^{j(A+B)}$ and compare real parts to get $\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B$.

blocks.text: Topic B: Find the general solution

[Week 2 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/08d203f6-a2b5-41b9-adfd-a14e22fb03d8#68929800-f011-4be7-a85a-29543465ed52) [Week 2 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/08d203f6-a2b5-41b9-adfd-a14e22fb03d8#49e5b3a7-1038-4f16-a4cc-2170fbbd61dc)

This is the core of the midterm: you are given an ODE (ordinary differential equation) and must find $y(t)$. There are seven methods, B1–B7. Which one works depends only on what the equation looks like, so the first move is always to **name the equation**.
**Step 1: name it.** Ask these five questions:

rows: Do $y,y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}$ appear only to the first power, never multiplied together or inside a function? ($t$ may appear anywhere.)
With every $y$-term on the left, is the right side $0$?
Are the numbers in front of $y,y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}$ constants?
Is $t$ missing from the equation completely?

blocks.text: **Step 2: pick the method.**

rows: integrating factor that makes it exact
2nd order, $t$ in the coefficients, one solution $y_1$ given

blocks.text: **Step 3: fix the constants.** Every method ends with a **general solution**: a formula with arbitrary constants.

items: 1st order: one constant, $C$. One condition, like $y(1)=2$, fixes it.
2nd order: two constants, $c_1,c_2$. Two conditions fix them: usually $y(0)$ and $y^{\prime}(0)$.
A problem with a condition is an **initial value problem** (IVP). Substitute the condition into the general solution and solve for the constant.

blocks.text: **Checking a solution** (a Week 2 question type): substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the ODE. It is a solution if the two sides match for **every** $t$. For an IVP, also check the starting value.

blocks.title: Problem 6 · W2 · Name it, then route it · lecture Example 2.1 and others
blocks.prompt:
For each equation, give its order, and say whether it is linear, homogeneous, constant-coefficient and autonomous. Then name the subtopic (B1–B7) that solves it.

(a) $t^3y^{\prime\prime}+e^ty^{\prime}+y=0$

(b) $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{y^2}{t^3}$

(c) $y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}+5y=10$

(d) $\dfrac{di}{dt}+5i=50$

(e) $(t-y)\,dt-(t+y)\,dy=0$

steps.explanation: (a) Highest derivative $y^{\prime\prime}$; $y$ terms are first power with $t$-only coefficients; right side 0; coefficients $t^3,e^t$ vary; $t$ appears. 2nd order, linear, homogeneous, **not** constant-coefficient, not autonomous → [B7](#b7) (once one solution is given).
(b) $y^2$ is not first power, so nonlinear; $t$ appears. It splits as $\frac{1}{t^3}\cdot y^2$ → [B1](#b1).
(c) 2nd order, linear, right side $10\neq0$ so **non**homogeneous, constant coefficients, autonomous → [B6](#b6).
(d) 1st order, linear, nonhomogeneous, constant coefficients, autonomous → [B2](#b2) (it also separates: $\frac{di}{50-5i}=dt$).
(e) As $y^{\prime}=\frac{t-y}{t+y}$: $y$ sits in a denominator, so nonlinear. In $M\,dt+N\,dy$ form, test exactness → [B3](#b3).

blocks.answer: (a) 2nd, linear, homogeneous, variable coefficients → B7. (b) 1st, nonlinear → B1. (c) 2nd, linear, nonhomogeneous, constant → B6. (d) 1st, linear, constant → B2. (e) 1st, nonlinear → B3.

blocks.title: Problem 7 · W2 · Check, then pick the member that fits
blocks.prompt: Which of $y=t^2$, $\;y=t^2+1$, $\;y=5t^2$ solve $ty^{\prime}-2y=0$? Which one also satisfies $y(1)=5$?
blocks.answer: $t^2$ and $5t^2$ are solutions (both are $Ct^2$); $t^2+1$ is not. Only $y=5t^2$ satisfies $y(1)=5$.

blocks.text: B1 · Separable equations
[Week 3 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/3d1ae4a9-687d-4654-873d-be3439faea2f#c40cdedd-01db-45b4-9498-4c4929ba8f49)
**The simplest case.** If you can move every $y$ to one side and every $t$ to the other, you can integrate each side on its own.
A first-order ODE is **separable** when it can be written as:

items: $g(t)$ = a part with only $t$ in it
$h(y)$ = a part with only $y$ in it

blocks.text: Example: $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{y^2}{t^3}$ has $g=\dfrac{1}{t^3}$ and $h=y^2$. Not separable: $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=t+y$, because a **sum** can’t be split into a product (that one goes to [B2](#b2)).
An equation already written as $M(t)\,dt+N(y)\,dy=0$, with only $t$ in $M$ and only $y$ in $N$, is separated already.
**Method:**

items: **Separate:** divide by $h(y)$ and multiply by $dt$:  $\dfrac{dy}{h(y)}=g(t)\,dt$.
**Integrate** both sides. Write one constant $C$, on the $t$ side.
**Condition:** substitute the given point to find $C$.
**Solve for $y$** if you can. If you can’t, the implicit answer (like $y^2+3=6(t^2+1)$) is a full answer.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here:**

rows: $e^{C}$ is just another constant; $\ln A+\ln B=\ln(AB)$

blocks.text: **Dividing by $h(y)$ hides constant solutions.** If $h(y_0)=0$ for a number $y_0$, then $y=y_0$ is a solution too. For $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{y^2}{t^3}$, $y=0$ is a solution that the separated formula misses.

**Bonus (skip-safe): why separating is allowed.** Divide by $h$: $\dfrac{1}{h(y)}\dfrac{dy}{dt}=g(t)$. Integrate both sides with respect to $t$. By the chain rule, $\int\dfrac{1}{h(y)}\dfrac{dy}{dt}\,dt=\int\dfrac{1}{h(y)}\,dy$. Writing “$dy$” and “$dt$” as separate pieces is shorthand for exactly this.

blocks.title: Example 2 · W3 · Separate after factoring · lecture Example 3.3
blocks.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{3t+ty^2}{y+t^2y}$, $\;y(1)=3$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** factor top and bottom; it becomes $g(t)\,h(y)$, so separable.
**Integrate:** both are “top = half the derivative of bottom”.
Multiply by 2 and exponentiate; $e^{2c}$ becomes a new constant $C_1$.
Solve for $y$; take the $+$ root because $y(1)=3>0$.

blocks.title: Problem 8 · W3 · Separate and use a starting value · Pre-tutorial 3(a)
blocks.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac{t}{y}$, $\;y=2$ when $t=1$.

steps.explanation: Solve for $y$, keeping the $+$ root since $y(1)=2>0$.

blocks.answer: $y=\sqrt{5-t^2}$ (a circle of radius $\sqrt5$, upper half), valid for $-\sqrt5<t<\sqrt5$.

blocks.title: Problem 9 · W3 · A general solution with a power · lecture Example 3.2
blocks.prompt: Find the general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac{y^2}{t^3}$.
blocks.answer: $\dfrac1y=\dfrac{1}{2t^2}+C$, i.e. $y=\dfrac{2t^2}{1+2Ct^2}$. Also $y=0$ (the constant solution lost by dividing by $y^2$).

blocks.title: Problem 10 · W3 · An exponential of y
blocks.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2t\,e^{-y}$, $\;y(0)=0$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** $2t\cdot e^{-y}$: separable. Dividing by $e^{-y}$ is multiplying by $e^{y}$.

blocks.title: Problem 11 · W3 · Differential form · Pre-tutorial 3(b)

steps.explanation: **Type:** each term is (t-part)(y-part), so dividing by $(y^2+1)(t^2+2)$ separates it.
**Integrate:** both are “top = derivative of bottom” (times $\frac32$ and $\frac12$).
Multiply by 2, then combine the logs: $3\ln A+\ln B=\ln(A^3B)$.

blocks.title: Problem 12 · W3 · Collect before separating · lecture Example 3.4
blocks.prompt: Solve $y\,dt+(t^3y^2+t^3)\,dy=0$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** factor $t^3$ out of the $dy$ term: $y\,dt+t^3(y^2+1)\,dy=0$. Dividing by $t^3y$ separates it.

blocks.text: B2 · Linear equations: the integrating factor
[Week 3 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/3d1ae4a9-687d-4654-873d-be3439faea2f#a43fc96e-8dc5-4a1e-bfdf-bf1acf01f98b)

**What if you can’t separate the variables?** $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=t-y$ won’t split into ($t$-part)×($y$-part), so [B1](#b1) fails. But if the equation is **linear**, an integrating factor solves it every time.
First-order linear equations can be written as:

items: $a(t)$ = the coefficient of $y$: everything multiplying $y$, **sign included**
$f(t)$ = the forcing: everything left over, with no $y$ in it

blocks.text: Examples:

items: $y^{\prime}=t-y$ → move $y$ left: $y^{\prime}+y=t$. So $a(t)=1$, $f(t)=t$.
$ty^{\prime}+2y=t^2$ → divide by $t$: $y^{\prime}+\frac2t\,y=t$. So $a(t)=\frac2t$, $f(t)=t$.

blocks.text: Get $y^{\prime}$ **alone** first (coefficient 1). Read $a(t)$ only after dividing: in $ty^{\prime}+2y=t^2$, $a(t)$ is $\frac2t$, not $2$.
**The integrating factor.** An integrating factor is a special function $\mu(t)$ that we multiply the entire equation by, to turn its left side into **one derivative**. The formula is:
After multiplying by $\mu$, the left side is exactly $(\mu y)^{\prime}$, so the equation becomes:
Integrate both sides:
**Method:**

items: **Standard form:** get $y^{\prime}$ alone; read $a(t)$ and $f(t)$.
**Integrating factor:** $\mu=e^{\int a\,dt}$. Leave out the $+C$ in this integral.
**Rewrite:** $(\mu y)^{\prime}=\mu f$.
**Integrate:** $\mu y=\int\mu f\,dt+C$. This is where the constant goes; don’t forget it.
**Divide by $\mu$**, then use the condition to find $C$.

blocks.text:
```steps
title "The method on y′ + 2y = 4"
$$ y'+2y=4 $$
Standard form already: $a=2$, $f=4$.
$$ \mu=e^{\int2\,dt}=\hl{e^{2t}} $$
Integrating factor.
$$ \hl{e^{2t}}y'+\hl{2e^{2t}}y=\hl{4e^{2t}} $$
Multiply every term by $\mu$.
$$ \hl{\big(e^{2t}y\big)^{\prime}}=4e^{2t} $$
The left side is one derivative (product rule backwards).
$$ e^{2t}y=2e^{2t}+\hl{C} $$
Integrate both sides: $\int4e^{2t}dt=2e^{2t}$.
$$ y=2+Ce^{-2t} $$
Divide by $e^{2t}$.
```
**Calculus you need here:**

rows: integration by parts; check by differentiating

blocks.text: **Shortcut for constant $a=k$ and constant $f=F$:** $\;y=\dfrac{F}{k}+Ce^{-kt}$. Every RC and RL circuit equation has this shape (see [D1](#d1)).

**Bonus (skip-safe): why does the integrating factor work?** Recall the **product rule** from calculus: $(\mu y)^{\prime}=\mu y^{\prime}+\mu^{\prime} y$. With $\mu=e^{\int a\,dt}$, the chain rule gives $\mu^{\prime}=a\,\mu$. So

$$
(\mu y)^{\prime}=\mu y^{\prime}+a\mu y=\mu\,(y^{\prime}+ay)
$$

which is exactly $\mu$ times the left side of the equation. Multiplying by $\mu$ turns “$y^{\prime}+ay$” into a single derivative you can integrate.
**Both separable and linear?** For example $y^{\prime}=(8t+3)y$, or any equation with constant $a$ and $f$. Then either method works: separating is usually faster.

blocks.text: B3 · Exact equations

[Week 4 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/ce2fa611-8b68-46a9-b6ca-653ae9c59aee#c9f71086-78d7-4bc3-a405-e0c6375fb6ca) [Week 4 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/ce2fa611-8b68-46a9-b6ca-653ae9c59aee#954310f2-d355-42ff-bd75-4e6b1d00f02d)

**When the equation comes in “$dt$ and $dy$” form.** Some first-order equations are neither separable nor linear, but their left side is the change of one hidden function $U(t,y)$. Then the solution is simply $U(t,y)=C$.
Write the equation with everything on the left:

items: $M$ = everything multiplying $dt$, **sign included**
$N$ = everything multiplying $dy$, **sign included**

blocks.text: Examples:

items: $y^{\prime}=\dfrac{t-y}{t+y}$ → cross-multiply: $(t+y)\,dy=(t-y)\,dt$ → move all left: $(t-y)\,dt-(t+y)\,dy=0$. So $M=t-y$, $N=-(t+y)$.

blocks.text: Moving the $dy$ term across the $=$ sign flips its sign. In $y^{\prime}=\frac{t-y}{t+y}$, $N$ is $-(t+y)$, not $t+y$. One wrong sign makes the test fail.
**The exactness test.** The equation is **exact** when the cross derivatives match:
Then there is a function $U(t,y)$ with
and the general solution is
**Method:**

items: **Rewrite** as $M\,dt+N\,dy=0$ (everything on the left).
**Test:** is $M_y=N_t$? ($M_y$ means $\partial M/\partial y$.) If not, go to [B4](#b4).
**Integrate $M$ in $t$:** $U=\int M\,dt+f(y)$. The “constant” is a whole function $f(y)$.
**Match $N$:** differentiate that $U$ in $y$, set it equal to $N$, solve for $f^{\prime}(y)$, integrate.
**Answer:** $U(t,y)=C$. Use the condition to find $C$.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here** (partial derivatives: hold the other letter fixed, like a number):

rows: $t$ is a constant: its derivative is 0
integrate in $t$ with $y$ fixed; anything with only $y$ vanishes under $\partial/\partial t$, so the constant is $f(y)$

blocks.text: **Bonus (skip-safe): why the test works, and what the answer means.** If $U$ exists, then $M_y=U_{ty}$ and $N_t=U_{yt}$. Mixed partial derivatives are equal, so $M_y=N_t$ must hold. Along a solution, $dU=U_t\,dt+U_y\,dy=M\,dt+N\,dy=0$: $U$ never changes. So each solution is a **level curve** $U(t,y)=C$ of the surface $z=U(t,y)$.

Slide $C$: the plane cuts the surface along one solution curve (an ellipse), drawn again on the floor.

blocks.title: Problem 19 · W4 · Test before you integrate · lecture exercise (d)
blocks.prompt: Is $y^{\prime}=\dfrac{t}{t+y}$ exact?

steps.explanation: **Type:** a slope formula: rewrite it in $M\,dt+N\,dy=0$ form first.

$0\neq-1$: **not exact**. The next move would be [B4](#b4), but neither of its ratios works here: $\frac{M_y-N_t}{N}=-\frac{1}{t+y}$ has both letters, and $\frac{N_t-M_y}{M}=-\frac1t$ has no $y$. The lecture stops at “not exact”.

blocks.title: Problem 21 · W4 · The sign trap · lecture exercise (c)
blocks.prompt: Solve $2ty\,y^{\prime}=t^2-y^2$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** write $y^{\prime}=\frac{dy}{dt}$, multiply by $dt$ and move the $dy$ term left: it becomes **negative**.

blocks.text: B4 · Not exact: make it exact with an integrating factor
[Week 4 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/ce2fa611-8b68-46a9-b6ca-653ae9c59aee#ebb7e8ad-4fda-4034-97dc-a9c048d71335)
**What if the exactness test fails?** Multiply the whole equation by a function $\mu$ (an **integrating factor**) chosen so that the new equation passes the test. Then finish with [B3](#b3).
Start from $M\,dt+N\,dy=0$ with $M_y\neq N_t$, and compute the **mismatch**:
**Theorem 1.** If this ratio depends on $t$ only, call it $f(t)$:
**Theorem 2.** If this ratio depends on $y$ only, call it $g(y)$:
**Memory aid:**

items: Theorem 1 divides the mismatch by $N$ and must leave only $t$.
Theorem 2 divides by $M$, with the subtraction **flipped** ($N_t-M_y$), and must leave only $y$.

blocks.text: **Method:**

items: **Test:** $M_y\neq N_t$ (otherwise it is already exact: [B3](#b3)).
**Ratios:** compute both. Keep the one that depends on a single letter.
**Integrating factor:** $\mu=e^{\int f\,dt}$ or $\mu=e^{\int g\,dy}$ (no $+C$ needed).
**Multiply the whole equation** by $\mu$: both $M$ and $N$.
**Re-test** (it must pass now), then solve with the [B3](#b3) steps.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here:**

**Bonus (skip-safe): where Theorem 1 comes from.** Multiply by $\mu(t)$ and ask for the new equation to pass the test: $(\mu M)_y=(\mu N)_t$, i.e. $\mu M_y=\mu^{\prime} N+\mu N_t$. Rearranged:

$$
\dfrac{\mu^{\prime}}{\mu}=\dfrac{M_y-N_t}{N}
$$

A $\mu$ depending on $t$ alone can only exist if the right side depends on $t$ alone. Then $\ln\mu=\int f\,dt$. Theorem 2 is the same argument with $\mu(y)$.

blocks.text: B5 · Second order, constant coefficients: the characteristic equation
[Week 5 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/0c7a77fe-aeed-47a8-b1c3-4967d73eea21#92fa557c-ab2a-49cb-a238-b9f4e76fa0b8)

**Now the equation has $y^{\prime\prime}$.** When every coefficient is a plain number, one guess solves it: $y=e^{st}$. Each derivative just brings out another $s$, so the whole ODE turns into a quadratic in $s$.
Second-order linear homogeneous equations with constant coefficients look like:

items: $a,b,c$ = numbers (constants), with $a\neq0$
right side $=0$ (homogeneous). If it isn’t $0$, you also need [B6](#b6).

blocks.text: Reading off the characteristic equation (replace $y^{\prime\prime}\to s^2$, $y^{\prime}\to s$, $y\to1$):

items: $y^{\prime\prime}+3y^{\prime}+2y=0$ → $s^2+3s+2=0$
$4y^{\prime\prime}+4y^{\prime}+y=0$ → $4s^2+4s+1=0$
$y^{\prime\prime}+9y=0$ → $s^2+9=0$ (no $y^{\prime}$ term, so no $s$ term)

blocks.text: **The characteristic equation.** Its roots decide the form of the solution:
Solve it by factoring, or with the quadratic formula:
If $b^2-4ac<0$, the square root is of a negative number: $\sqrt{-16}=j4$. See [Topic A](#topic-a) for complex roots.
The last two columns are the time saver: with conditions at $t=0$ you get the two equations for $A$ and $B$ without differentiating. For conditions at any other time, differentiate $y(t)$ yourself.
**Method:**

items: **Characteristic equation:** replace $y^{\prime\prime}\to s^2$, $y^{\prime}\to s$, $y\to1$.
**Roots:** factor, or use the quadratic formula.
**Form:** pick the row of the table that matches the roots.
**Conditions:** $y(0)$ and $y^{\prime}(0)$ give two equations; solve for $A$ and $B$.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here** (to differentiate the forms yourself):

```graph
title "Slide $k$ through 1: the same start, three kinds of response"
x 0 8 label="$t$"
y -0.6 1.2 label="$y$"
slider k 0 5 0.5 step=0.05 label="$k$" animate
let d "sqrt(abs(1-k))"
let s1 "-1+d"
let s2 "-1-d"
curve "if(k<0.999, (s2*exp(s1*x)-s1*exp(s2*x))/(s2-s1), if(k>1.001, exp(-x)*(cos(d*x)+sin(d*x)/d), (1+x)*exp(-x)))" label="$y(t)$" color=1
hline "0"
readout "$b^2-4ac=4-4k$" "4-4*k"
caption "$y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}+ky=0$ with $y(0)=1$, $y^{\prime}(0)=0$. For $k<1$: two real roots, a smooth decay. At $k=1$: a repeated root. For $k>1$: complex roots, and the solution oscillates inside a decaying envelope $e^{-t}$."
```

**Bonus (skip-safe): why $e^{st}$ turns the ODE into a quadratic.** Put $y=e^{st}$, $y^{\prime}=se^{st}$, $y^{\prime\prime}=s^2e^{st}$ into the ODE:

$$
as^2e^{st}+bse^{st}+ce^{st}=(as^2+bs+c)\,e^{st}=0
$$

Since $e^{st}$ is never zero, the bracket must be: that is the characteristic equation. Complex roots give real answers through Euler, $e^{(\sigma\pm j\omega)t}=e^{\sigma t}(\cos\omega t\pm j\sin\omega t)$. The extra $t$ for a repeated root comes from reduction of order ([B7](#b7)).

blocks.text: B6 · Undetermined coefficients
[Week 6 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/357f26bd-d16c-4769-af0a-d1b2f535d62e#77a5aea3-a3f4-4738-a817-01c3f18cfdae)

**What if the right side isn’t zero?** The forcing $g(t)$ (a source, in a circuit) pushes the solution. The [B5](#b5) solutions only ever produce $0$ on the right, so they need a partner that produces $g(t)$.
Second-order linear equations with constant coefficients and a forcing term look like:

items: left side = the same as in B5 (numbers $a,b,c$)
$g(t)$ = the **forcing**: everything with no $y$ in it, moved to the right

blocks.text: The solution is always built from two pieces:

items: $y_c$ = the **complementary solution**: the general solution with $g$ replaced by $0$ (that is [B5](#b5)). It holds the two constants $c_1,c_2$.
$y_p$ = a **particular solution**: any one function that produces $g(t)$. No constants.

blocks.text: Mini example: $y^{\prime\prime}+y=3$. Then $y_c=c_1\sin t+c_2\cos t$, and $y_p=3$ works ($0+3=3$). So $y=3+c_1\sin t+c_2\cos t$.
**Finding $y_p$: guess its form from $g(t)$.** Write a guess with unknown coefficients ($A,B,\dots$), substitute it, and match coefficients. The guess copies the shape of $g$:

**The $\times t$ rule.** If any term of your guess already appears in $y_c$, substituting it gives $0$, so it can never produce $g$. **Multiply that guess by $t$.** If it is still in $y_c$ (a repeated root), multiply by $t^2$.
**Method:**

items: **Complementary:** solve the equation with $g=0$ ([B5](#b5)) to get $y_c$.
**Guess:** take $y_p$’s form from the table. Compare it with $y_c$; apply the $\times t$ rule if needed.
**Substitute** $y_p$ into the ODE and **match coefficients** (constants, each $\cos$, each $\sin$, each power of $t$). Solve for $A,B,\dots$
**Add:** $y=y_c+y_p$.
**Conditions** on the **whole** $y$, never on $y_c$ or $y_p$ alone.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here:**

rows: product rule twice, for a $\times t$ guess

blocks.text: **Bonus (skip-safe): why $y=y_c+y_p$ works.** The left side is linear: put in $y_c+y_p$ and you get (what $y_c$ gives) + (what $y_p$ gives) $=0+g=g$. And $y_c$ still carries two free constants, enough to meet any two conditions. The $\times t$ rule has the same root: a term of $y_c$ gives $0$ on the left, so it is useless as a guess.

blocks.text: B7 · Reduction of order
[Week 6 · Topic 1](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/357f26bd-d16c-4769-af0a-d1b2f535d62e#400c9eda-6dcb-4cf4-9c21-265384342cb1)

**What if the coefficients have $t$ in them?** Like $y^{\prime\prime}-ty^{\prime}+y=0$. The characteristic equation ([B5](#b5)) only works when the coefficients are numbers. But if the question **gives you one solution** $y_1$, reduction of order finds the second one.
Write the equation with $y^{\prime\prime}$ alone (divide by its coefficient):

items: $p(t)$ = the coefficient of $y^{\prime}$ (sign included)
$q(t)$ = the coefficient of $y$
$y_1(t)$ = the solution you are given. Check it first: it must give $0$.

blocks.text: Mini examples:

items: $y^{\prime\prime}-ty^{\prime}+y=0$ with $y_1=t$: here $p=-t$, $q=1$. Check: $0-t\cdot1+t=0$ ✓.
$t^2y^{\prime\prime}-3ty^{\prime}+4y=0$ with $y_1=t^2$: divide by $t^2$, so $p=-\frac3t$, $q=\frac4{t^2}$.

blocks.text: **The idea.** Look for the second solution as the known one times an unknown function $v(t)$:
Substituting makes every plain-$v$ term cancel, so only $v^{\prime}$ and $v^{\prime\prime}$ are left. Setting $z=v^{\prime}$ turns that into a **first-order** equation: the order went down by one.
**Method:**

items: **Substitute** $y=y_1v$, with $y^{\prime}=y_1^{\prime} v+y_1v^{\prime}$ and $y^{\prime\prime}=y_1^{\prime\prime} v+2y_1^{\prime} v^{\prime}+y_1v^{\prime\prime}$.
**Collect** terms: the plain-$v$ terms cancel, because $y_1$ is a solution.
**Set $z=v^{\prime}$** and solve the first-order equation for $z$ (usually separable, [B1](#b1); or linear, [B2](#b2)).
**Integrate:** $v=\int z\,dt$, plus a constant.
**Multiply back:** $y=y_1v$. The constant from step 4 gives back $C\,y_1$, the solution you started with.

blocks.text: **Check with the formula.** Reduction of order always ends at
Use it to check your answer, or as a shortcut if the question allows it.
**Calculus you need here:**

rows: product rule twice; the middle terms combine
leave it as an integral: that is a full answer

blocks.text: **Bonus (skip-safe): why the plain-$v$ terms cancel.** After substituting, collect everything that multiplies $v$ itself: it is $v\,(y_1^{\prime\prime}+p\,y_1^{\prime}+q\,y_1)$. The bracket is the ODE applied to $y_1$, which is $0$ because $y_1$ is a solution.

The professor’s example, step by step:

```steps
title "Lecture: reduce y″ − t y′ + y = 0, given y₁ = t"
$$ y''-ty'+y=0,\qquad y_1=t $$
Check: $y_1=t$ gives $0-t+t=0$.
$$ y=\hl{tv} $$
Multiply the known solution by an unknown $v$.
$$ y'=\hl{v+tv'},\qquad y''=\hl{2v'+tv''} $$
Product rule (calculus table).
$$ (2v'+tv'')-t(v+tv')+tv=0 $$
Substitute all three into the ODE.
$$ \hl{tv''+(2-t^2)v'}=0 $$
Collect terms. The $-tv$ and $+tv$ cancel.
$$ t\hl{z'}+(2-t^2)\hl{z}=0 $$
Set $z=v^{\prime}$: first order in $z$.
```

blocks.text: Topic C: Does exactly one solution exist?

[Week 3 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/3d1ae4a9-687d-4654-873d-be3439faea2f#8c746b9b-2fbf-48f4-8a2d-704a643bdcf7) [Week 5 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/0c7a77fe-aeed-47a8-b1c3-4967d73eea21#b4f41ebe-f4f6-4d5d-816d-ceaa37811b8f)

Some midterm questions ask **whether** a problem has exactly one solution, or **where** it is guaranteed, without solving anything. Two theorems answer that: one for first-order equations, one for second-order linear ones.
The answer is always found the same way: write the equation in a standard form, then look for the places where something breaks (division by zero, a log of a negative, a square root of a negative).
C1 · First order: is there exactly one solution through this point?
[Week 3 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/3d1ae4a9-687d-4654-873d-be3439faea2f#8c746b9b-2fbf-48f4-8a2d-704a643bdcf7)
**When:** the question gives $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=F(t,y)$ and a starting point $(t_0,y_0)$, and asks if a unique solution passes through it.
Write the equation with the derivative alone:

items: $F(t,y)$ = everything on the right side once $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ is alone
$\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}$ = its **partial derivative** in $y$: differentiate in $y$ while treating $t$ as a constant

blocks.text: **The theorem** (Spiegel, used in the Week 3 lecture):
If $F$ and $\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}$ are both continuous (finite, defined) in a region around $(t_0,y_0)$, then **exactly one** solution passes through $(t_0,y_0)$.

items: **Conditions hold** → existence and uniqueness are guaranteed (near $t_0$).
**Conditions fail** → the theorem says **nothing**. There may be no solution, one, or many. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary.

blocks.text: Mini examples:

items: $y^{\prime}=t^2+3ty$: $F_y=3t$. Both are fine everywhere → unique through **every** point.
$y^{\prime}=\dfrac{t}{y}$: $F_y=-\dfrac{t}{y^2}$. Both break on the line $y=0$ → guaranteed only at points with $y_0\neq0$.

blocks.text: **Method:**

items: **Write $F$:** get $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ alone.
**Differentiate:** find $\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}$, holding $t$ fixed.
**Find the bad set:** where is $F$ or $\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}$ undefined (divide by 0, $\ln$ of $\le0$, $\sqrt{\ }$ of $<0$, $y^{-1/2}$ at $y=0$)?
**Check the point:** is $(t_0,y_0)$ away from the bad set? Yes → unique solution. No → no conclusion.

blocks.text: **Calculus you need here:**

```graph
title "$y^{\prime}=\sqrt{y}$: one solution through $(1,4)$, many through $(1,0)$"
x -1 5 label="$t$"
y -0.5 6 label="$y$"
field "sqrt(max(y,0))" density=18
hline "0" label="$y=0$ is a solution" color=1
family c 1 3 0.5 "if(x>c,(x-c)^2/4,0)" color=2 label="also solutions through $(1,0)$"
curve "((x+3)/2)^2" from=-3 label="the only solution through $(1,4)$" color=3
point "1" "0" color=1
point "1" "4" color=3
caption "At $y=0$, $\partial F/\partial y=1/(2\sqrt y)$ is undefined, so the theorem gives no guarantee, and indeed many curves leave $(1,0)$: each stays at 0, then rises as $(t-c)^2/4$. Above the axis everything is smooth and the solution is unique."
```

**Bonus (skip-safe): why a blown-up $\partial F/\partial y$ allows several solutions.** $\partial F/\partial y$ measures how strongly nearby curves are pushed apart. If it stays finite, two solutions that start together can never separate. At $y=0$ for $\sqrt y$ it is infinite, so a curve can “peel off” the axis at any moment.

blocks.title: Problem 38 · W3 · A strip, not a point
blocks.prompt: For $(t-3)\,y^{\prime}+(\ln t)\,y=2t$, $\;y(1)=2$, find the region containing the starting point where the theorem applies. Do not solve.

steps.explanation: **Bad set:** $\ln t$ needs $t>0$; division needs $t\neq3$. Nothing restricts $y$.

blocks.answer: The strip $0<t<3$ (all $y$). The start $(1,2)$ is inside it, so exactly one solution passes through it.

blocks.text: C2 · Second order linear: interval, zero start, independent solutions
[Week 5 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/0c7a77fe-aeed-47a8-b1c3-4967d73eea21#b4f41ebe-f4f6-4d5d-816d-ceaa37811b8f)

**When:** a second-order **linear** equation with two conditions $y(t_0)$, $y^{\prime}(t_0)$, and the question asks on what interval exactly one solution exists, or whether two given solutions can build the general solution.
First divide by the coefficient of $y^{\prime\prime}$ so it stands alone:

items: $p(t)$ = the coefficient of $y^{\prime}$ (after dividing)
$q(t)$ = the coefficient of $y$ (after dividing)
$g(t)$ = the forcing (after dividing)

blocks.text: **The theorem.** If $p$, $q$ and $g$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$, then for **any** values of $y(t_0)$ and $y^{\prime}(t_0)$ there is **exactly one** solution, and it exists on the **whole** interval $I$.

items: The largest such $I$ runs from the nearest “trouble point” on the left of $t_0$ to the nearest on the right.
Constant coefficients ($ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=g$ with continuous $g$): no trouble points, $I$ is the whole real line.

blocks.text: Mini example: $t\,y^{\prime\prime}+y=0$ → divide by $t$: $q=\dfrac1t$, trouble at $t=0$. For $t_0=5$: $I=(0,\infty)$. For $t_0=-2$: $I=(-\infty,0)$.
**Method (interval):**

items: **Divide** by the coefficient of $y^{\prime\prime}$; read $p,q,g$.
**Trouble points:** where $p$, $q$ or $g$ is undefined (zero denominators, $\ln$ of $\le0$, …).
**Pick the piece** of the $t$-axis between trouble points that contains $t_0$. Use open ends.

blocks.text: **Zero start.** If the equation is linear and **homogeneous** ($g=0$) and both conditions are zero, $y(t_0)=0$ and $y^{\prime}(t_0)=0$, then:
Reason in one line: $y=0$ obviously solves it and fits both conditions, and the theorem says there is only one solution. No solving needed.
**Two solutions → the general solution?** If $y_1$ and $y_2$ solve the same homogeneous linear equation, compute their **Wronskian**:

items: $W\neq0$ → $y_1,y_2$ are **independent**, and $y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2$ is the general solution.
$W=0$ → one is a multiple of the other; they give only one real constant, so they are **not** enough.

blocks.text: This is why the repeated-root case in [B5](#b5) uses $(c_1+c_2t)e^{st}$ and not $c_1e^{st}+c_2e^{st}$.

**Bonus (skip-safe): why the Wronskian decides it.** Fitting $c_1y_1+c_2y_2$ to $y(t_0)$ and $y^{\prime}(t_0)$ gives two equations:

$$
c_1y_1+c_2y_2=y(t_0),\quad c_1y_1^{\prime}+c_2y_2^{\prime}=y^{\prime}(t_0)
$$

That $2\times2$ system has a unique answer exactly when its determinant $y_1y_2^{\prime}-y_1^{\prime} y_2=W$ is not zero. $W\neq0$ means every pair of starting values can be matched.

blocks.title: Problem 39 · W5 · Find the interval; do not solve
blocks.prompt: For $(t-1)\,y^{\prime\prime}+y^{\prime}+y=\ln t$, find the largest interval on which the theorem guarantees exactly one solution for (a) $t_0=2$, (b) $t_0=\tfrac12$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** existence and uniqueness, second-order linear. **Divide** by $t-1$.
**Trouble points:** $\ln t$ needs $t>0$; the denominator needs $t\neq1$. So the pieces are $(0,1)$ and $(1,\infty)$.
**Pick the piece:** $t_0=2$ is in $(1,\infty)$; $t_0=\tfrac12$ is in $(0,1)$.

blocks.title: Problem 40 · W5 · Which pair gives the general solution?
blocks.prompt: Both pairs solve $y^{\prime\prime}+4y^{\prime}+4y=0$: (a) $e^{-2t}$ and $3e^{-2t}$; (b) $e^{-2t}$ and $te^{-2t}$. Compute each Wronskian and decide which pair gives the general solution.

steps.explanation: $e^{-4t}$ is never zero, so pair (b) is independent.

blocks.answer: (a) $W=0$: not enough (they are multiples). (b) $W=e^{-4t}\neq0$: general solution $y=(c_1+c_2t)e^{-2t}$.

blocks.title: Problem 41 · W5 + W6 · The answer without solving
blocks.prompt: Solve $y^{\prime\prime}+t\,y^{\prime}+e^{t}\,y=0$, $\;y(0)=0$, $\;y^{\prime}(0)=0$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** looks unsolvable with our methods ($t$ and $e^t$ coefficients), but it is linear, homogeneous, with a **zero start**.
**Interval:** $p=t$, $q=e^t$, $g=0$ are continuous everywhere, so exactly one solution exists on the whole real line.

blocks.text: Topic D: Circuits → ODE → solution

[Week 2 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/08d203f6-a2b5-41b9-adfd-a14e22fb03d8#77c9c878-68d6-44e3-8f1e-2f68ba18701b) [Week 5 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/0c7a77fe-aeed-47a8-b1c3-4967d73eea21#d5ad9ba9-0ec5-4b62-acf5-b1c7e17d6463)
Every circuit question in this course is the same job: a switch moves (or a source changes) at $t=0$, and you need $v(t)$ or $i(t)$ afterwards.
The circuit hands you two things:

items: **the ODE**, from KVL or KCL after the switch;
**the starting values**, from the circuit before the switch.

blocks.text: Then Topic B solves the ODE, exactly as before.
**The element facts.** Everything in this topic comes from these three rows:

items: **DC steady state** = “the switch has been there **for a long time**”: nothing changes any more, so every $\frac{d}{dt}$ is 0.
$0^-$ = just before the switch moves; $0^+$ = just after.

blocks.text: So always solve for the quantity that **can’t jump**: $v_C$ in a capacitor circuit, $i_L$ in an inductor circuit. Get everything else (resistor currents, $i_C$, $v_L$) from it afterwards.
**What each element looks like at the three moments you need:**

```graph
title "A capacitor charging from $0\,\mathrm{V}$: its voltage is continuous, its current jumps"
x -1 5 label="$t/\tau$"
y -0.2 1.2 label="fraction of final value"
curve "if(x<0, 0, 1-exp(-x))" label="$v_C$: starts at 0, no jump" color=1
curve "if(x<0, 0, exp(-x))" label="$i_C$: 0 before, jumps at $t=0$" color=2
vline "0" label="switch closes" color=0
caption "Pre-tutorial 2 in picture form. Before the switch closes no current flows. Just after, $v_C$ is still 0, so all of the source current goes into the capacitor: $i_C$ jumps, $v_C$ doesn’t."
```
**The switching recipe** (every circuit problem):

items: **Before ($t<0$):** the switch has been in its old position for a long time, so the circuit is in DC steady state. Replace $C$ by an open circuit and $L$ by a short. Find $v_C(0^-)$ or $i_L(0^-)$.

**Just after ($t=0^+$):** carry them over: $v_C(0^+)=v_C(0^-)$, $i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)$. To find anything else at $0^+$, redraw the **new** circuit with $C$ as a voltage source $v_C(0^+)$ and $L$ as a current source $i_L(0^+)$, then use KVL/KCL.
**After ($t>0$):** in the new circuit, write KCL at a node or KVL around the loop. Replace $i_C$ by $C\frac{dv}{dt}$ and $v_L$ by $L\frac{di}{dt}$. That is the ODE.

**Solve:** one $L$ or $C$ → first order → [B2](#b2) (or the [D1](#d1) formula). An $L$ and a $C$ → second order → [B5](#b5) (no source) or [B6](#b6) (constant source), see [D2](#d2). The values from step 2 are the conditions.
**Check ($t\to\infty$):** DC steady state again ($C$ open, $L$ short). Your answer must approach this final value.

blocks.text: **Before and after are two different circuits.** Draw both. Use the old one only for step 1; write the ODE (step 3) from the new one, with only the parts still connected.

**Signs come from the drawn arrow.** If the reference arrow for $i_L$ points against the real current, the starting value is **negative**. Find the real direction first, then compare it with the arrow.

**Bonus (skip-safe): why $v_C$ and $i_L$ can’t jump.** If $v_C$ jumped, $\frac{dv}{dt}$ would be infinite, so $i=C\frac{dv}{dt}$ would be infinite: no real circuit supplies that. The same with $v=L\frac{di}{dt}$ for an inductor current. The stored energy $\frac12Cv^2$ or $\frac12Li^2$ cannot change instantly.
D1 · First-order RC and RL circuits

[Week 1 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/1cbac07a-cd02-48c2-8c30-c9829c4e06b2#ab5bf400-4411-4869-8d74-7790f8ee6f2c) [Week 2 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/08d203f6-a2b5-41b9-adfd-a14e22fb03d8#77c9c878-68d6-44e3-8f1e-2f68ba18701b) [Week 3 · Topic 2](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/3d1ae4a9-687d-4654-873d-be3439faea2f#a43fc96e-8dc5-4a1e-bfdf-bf1acf01f98b)
**When:** after the switch, the circuit has **one** capacitor or **one** inductor (after combining), plus resistors and DC sources. Then the ODE is first order, and it always has the same shape.
Call $x$ the quantity that can’t jump ($v_C$ or $i_L$). For $t>0$, KCL or KVL always gives:

items: $x$ = $v_C$ in an RC circuit, $i_L$ in an RL circuit
$\tau$ = the **time constant** (seconds): $\;\tau=R_{th}C\;$ or $\;\tau=\dfrac{L}{R_{th}}$
$x_f$ = the **final value** $x(\infty)$, from the DC steady state after the switch ($x_f=0$ if no source is left)
$R_{th}$ = the resistance the $C$ or $L$ “sees”: turn the sources off (voltage source → short, current source → open) and combine the resistors between its two terminals, in the $t>0$ circuit

blocks.text: This is a [B2](#b2) equation with constant $a=\frac1\tau$ and constant $f=\frac{x_f}{\tau}$. Its shortcut solution, with the starting value $x(0)=x_0$, is the one formula you need:
**Method** (the D0 recipe, specialised):

items: **$x_0$:** from the $t<0$ DC circuit ($C$ open, $L$ short), carried over to $0^+$.
**$x_f$:** from the $t\to\infty$ DC circuit, with the switch in its **new** position.
**$\tau$:** find $R_{th}$ seen by the $C$ or $L$ in the $t>0$ circuit; $\tau=R_{th}C$ or $L/R_{th}$.
**Plug in:** $x(t)=x_f+(x_0-x_f)e^{-t/\tau}$.
**Anything else** from $x(t)$: Ohm’s law, KCL, $i_C=C\frac{dv_C}{dt}$, $v_L=L\frac{di_L}{dt}$.

rows: no source is left after $t=0$: stored energy dies out
a DC source drives the circuit after $t=0$
$x_f$ from the new DC steady state

blocks.text: **Reading the curve:** after $1\tau$, $e^{-1}=37\%$ of the starting gap $x_0-x_f$ is left (63% done); after $2\tau$, 13.5%; after $5\tau$, under 1% (“done”).

```graph
title "Drag the sliders: the curve always heads for $x_f$, and the tangent at $t=0$ reaches $x_f$ at $t=\tau$"
x 0 8 label="$t$"
y -12 12 label="$x$"
slider x0 -10 10 10 step=1 label="$x_0$"
slider xf -10 10 2 step=1 label="$x_f$"
slider tau 0.2 3 1 step=0.1 label="$\tau$"
curve "xf+(x0-xf)*exp(-x/tau)" label="$x(t)=x_f+(x_0-x_f)e^{-t/\tau}$" color=1
curve "x0+(xf-x0)*x/tau" from=0 to="tau" label="tangent at $t=0$" color=0 dash
hline "xf" label="$x_f$" color=3
point "tau" "xf+(x0-xf)*exp(-1)" label="at $t=\tau$: 37% of the gap left" color=2
readout "$x(5\tau)$" "xf+(x0-xf)*exp(-5)"
caption "Set $x_f=0$ for a natural response. A bigger $\tau$ (bigger $RC$ or $L/R$) means a slower circuit."
```
**Formulas you’ll also need:**

**Bonus (skip-safe): where the formula comes from (the lecture’s RC step response).** A current source $I_s$, a resistor $R$ and a capacitor $C$ in parallel. KCL at the top node: capacitor current plus resistor current equals the source current:

$$
C\dfrac{dv}{dt}+\dfrac{v}{R}=I_s\quad\Rightarrow\quad\dfrac{dv}{dt}+\dfrac{v}{RC}=\dfrac{I_s}{C}
$$

That is the standard form with $\tau=RC$ and $x_f=RI_s$, so $v=RI_s+(V_0-RI_s)e^{-t/RC}$. It is [B2](#b2) with constant coefficients, and it also separates ([B1](#b1)), as the lecture showed for the RL circuit.

blocks.title: Example 9 · W3 · Circuit → ODE → answer · lecture §1.1
blocks.prompt:
The switch closes at $t=0$; the inductor carries no current before. Find $i(t)$ for $t\ge0$.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$100\,\mathrm{V}$"
S1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$t=0$" action=close
R1 3,3 -> 6,3 "$10\,\Omega$" i="$i$"
L1 6,3 -> 6,0 "$2\,\mathrm{H}$" v="$v$"
wire 6,0 -> 0,0
ground 0,0
```

steps.explanation: **Type:** one inductor, one DC source → first-order RL step response. Solve for $i$ (the inductor current).
**Before:** the switch is open, so no current: $i(0^-)=0$, and $i(0^+)=0$ (it can’t jump).
**After:** KVL around the loop: the source equals the resistor voltage plus the inductor voltage.
Divide by $L=2$ to get the standard form: $\frac1\tau=5$, so $\tau=0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ (check: $L/R=2/10$).
**Final value:** at $t\to\infty$ the inductor is a short, so $i_f=100/10=10\,\mathrm{A}$.

blocks.answer: $i(t)=10\big(1-e^{-5t}\big)\,\mathrm{A}$, the same answer the integrating factor gave (Problem in [B2](#b2)).

blocks.title: Problem 42 · W1 · RL natural response · Pre-tutorial 1
blocks.prompt:
The switch has been closed for a long time and opens at $t=0$. With $L=8\,\mathrm{mH}$, $R=4\,\Omega$ and $I_s=4\,\mathrm{A}$, find the numerical expression for $i(t)$, $t\ge0$, and sketch it.

```schematic
I1 0,0 -> 0,3 "$I_s=4\,\mathrm{A}$"
wire 0,3 -> 3,3
R1 3,3 -> 3,0 "$R_0$"
S1 3,3 -> 6,3 "$t=0$" action=open
L1 6,3 -> 6,0 "$8\,\mathrm{mH}$" i="$i$"
wire 6,3 -> 9,3
R2 9,3 -> 9,0 "$4\,\Omega$" v="$v$"
wire 9,0 -> 0,0
ground 0,0
```

steps.explanation: **Type:** after the switch opens, only the $L$–$R$ loop is left, with no source: RL **natural** response. Solve for $i$.
**Before:** DC steady state, so $L$ is a short. It shorts $R_0$ and $R$, so all of $I_s$ flows down through $L$.
**Sketch:** starts at 4 A, is $4e^{-1}\approx1.47\,\mathrm{A}$ at $t=2\,\mathrm{ms}$, and is essentially 0 after $5\tau=10\,\mathrm{ms}$.

blocks.title: Problem 43 · W2 · Can the capacitor current jump? · Pre-tutorial 2
blocks.prompt:
The capacitor is uncharged ($V_0=0$). The switch closes at $t=0$, with $I_s=2\,\mathrm{A}$ and $R=1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. Find the capacitor current at $t=0^-$ (switch open) and at $t=0^+$ (switch closed). Is there a discontinuity in the capacitor current, unlike the capacitor voltage?

```schematic
I1 0,0 -> 0,3 "$I_s=2\,\mathrm{A}$"
wire 0,3 -> 3,3
R1 3,3 -> 3,0 "$1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$" i="$v/R$"
S1 3,3 -> 6,3 "$t=0$" action=close
C1 6,3 -> 6,0 "$C$" v="$v$" i="$i_C$"
wire 6,0 -> 0,0
ground 0,0
```

steps.explanation: **Type:** a $0^-$/$0^+$ question: use “$v_C$ can’t jump”, then KCL at $0^+$.
**Before:** the switch is open, so the capacitor is disconnected.
**Just after:** $v(0^+)=v(0^-)=0$ (can’t jump). So the resistor current is $v/R=0$.
KCL at the top node: all of the source current must go into the capacitor.

blocks.answer: $i_C(0^-)=0$, $i_C(0^+)=2\,\mathrm{A}$: yes, the capacitor **current** jumps; the capacitor **voltage** stays continuous at 0.

blocks.prompt:
The switch has been in position $a$ for a long time. At $t=0$ it moves to position $b$ and stays there. Find the initial and final values of the capacitor voltage, the time constant for $t\ge0$, and $v_C(t)$ for $t\ge0$. (The $200\,\mathrm{V}$ source has its $-$ on top. The two $t=0$ switches are one two-position switch: at $t=0$ the contact at $a$ opens and the contact at $b$ closes.)

```schematic

R1 0,3 -> 2,3 "$10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$"
S1 2,3 -> 4,3 "$t=0$" action=open

S2 4,3 -> 6,3 "$t=0$" action=close

R4 8,3 -> 10,3 "$50\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$"

wire 10,0 -> 0,0

label 6,3 "$b$" above

```

steps.explanation: **Type:** one capacitor, a DC source after the switch: RC **step** response. Solve for $v_C$.
**Before (position $a$):** $C$ is open, so no current flows through $10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$: the capacitor holds the full source.

**After (position $b$):** replace everything right of $b$ by its Thévenin equivalent. With $C$ removed, no current flows in $12.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$; the divider gives the node voltage (the source’s top is at $-200\,\mathrm{V}$).
Sources off (the $200\,\mathrm{V}$ source becomes a short): $12.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ plus $150\parallel50$.
**Final value and time constant:** $C$ ends at $V_{th}$.

blocks.text: D2 · RLC circuits (second order)
[Week 5 · Topic 3](/courses/206af2a6-c1f1-4700-ac44-5eba708c676b/docs/0c7a77fe-aeed-47a8-b1c3-4967d73eea21#d5ad9ba9-0ec5-4b62-acf5-b1c7e17d6463)

**When the circuit has one inductor and one capacitor** (after combining), its equation is **second order**. The math is [B5](#b5) (and [B6](#b6) when a source stays on). The new part is getting the equation and the two starting values from the circuit.
Before anything, find the starting values with the switching recipe in [Topic D](#topic-d): $v_C(0^+)$ and $i_L(0^+)$ carry over from just before the switch.
**The two circuits you will meet:**

blocks.caption: Series RLC: one loop, one current $i$ through all four elements.
Parallel RLC: two nodes, one voltage $v$ across all three elements; all currents point down.

blocks.text: Both equations have the shape below, so the characteristic equation and its roots are:
**Compare $\alpha$ with $\omega_0$ to know the shape before solving.** These are the three root cases of [B5](#b5) with circuit names:
Here $\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\alpha^2}$ is the **damped frequency**: how fast an underdamped response oscillates.

```graph
title "Slide R through the three cases (series RLC, $L=1\,\mathrm{H}$, $C=0.25\,\mathrm{F}$)"
x 0 6 label="$t$ (s)"
y -8 11 label="$v_C$ (V)"
slider R 0 10 1 step=0.1 label="$R$ ($\Omega$)" animate
let a "R/2"
let wd "sqrt(abs(4-a^2))"
let s1 "-a+wd"
let s2 "-a-wd"
curve "if(abs(a-2)<0.001, 10*(1+2*t)*exp(-2*t), if(a<2, 10*exp(-a*t)*(cos(wd*t)+a/wd*sin(wd*t)), 10*(s2*exp(s1*t)-s1*exp(s2*t))/(s2-s1)))" label="$v_C(t)$, from $10\,\mathrm{V}$ with $i=0$" color=1
hline "0"
readout "$\alpha=R/2L$" "a"
readout "$\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$" "2"
caption "$\omega_0=2$ is fixed. $R<4$: $\alpha<\omega_0$, underdamped (it swings below zero). $R=4$: critically damped, the fastest return without overshoot. $R>4$: overdamped, a slow creep back. $R=0$: undamped, it never dies out."
```

**With a source that stays on** (a step response), the answer is a **final value** plus a part that dies out. The final value comes from the DC steady state ($C$ open, $L$ short): it is the constant $y_p$ of [B6](#b6). Fit the constants to $v_C=V_f+(\text{transient})$, not to the transient alone.
**Method:**

items: **Before:** DC steady state for $t<0$ gives $v_C(0^-)$ and $i_L(0^-)$.
**Starting values:** $v_C(0^+)=v_C(0^-)$, $i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)$, then the starting slope (table above).
**Equation:** series or parallel? Compute $\alpha$ and $\omega_0$; compare them to pick the form.
**Final value:** $0$ with no source; otherwise the DC steady state after the switch.
**Constants:** use the starting value and slope on the full expression (product rule for the slope).

blocks.text: **Units.** Convert $\mathrm{mH}$, $\mathrm{mF}$, $\mu\mathrm{F}$, $\mathrm{nF}$ to H and F before computing $\alpha$ and $\omega_0$. $1\,\mathrm{nF}=10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F}$, $1\,\mu\mathrm{F}=10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$, $1\,\mathrm{mH}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{H}$.

**Bonus (skip-safe): where the series equation comes from.** KVL around the loop, then replace the current by $Cv_C^{\prime}$:

```steps
$$ V_s=Ri+Li^{\prime}+v_C $$
KVL: the three element voltages add up to the source.
$$ i=\hl{Cv_C^{\prime}} $$
The loop current is the capacitor current.
$$ V_s=RC\,v_C^{\prime}+LC\,v_C^{\prime\prime}+v_C $$
Substitute the current and its derivative.
$$ v_C^{\prime\prime}+\hl{\dfrac RL}v_C^{\prime}+\hl{\dfrac1{LC}}v_C=\hl{\dfrac{V_s}{LC}} $$
Divide by $LC$.
```

For the parallel circuit, KCL at the top node is $Cv^{\prime}+i_L+\dfrac vR=0$. Differentiate once and use $i_L^{\prime}=\dfrac vL$.

blocks.title: Example 10 · W5 · A series step response · textbook P8.53
blocks.prompt:
The circuit has been in operation for a long time with $V_s=200\,\mathrm{V}$. At $t=0$ the source drops to $100\,\mathrm{V}$. Find $v_C(t)$ for $t\ge0$.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$200\to100\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$4\,\Omega$" i="$i$"
L1 3,3 -> 6,3 "$40\,\mathrm{mH}$"
C1 6,3 -> 6,0 "$10\,\mathrm{mF}$" v="$v_C$"
wire 6,0 -> 0,0
ground 0,0
```

steps.explanation: **Type:** one $L$, one $C$ in one loop with a source that stays on: series RLC step response.
**Before:** DC steady state, $C$ open so $i=0$. No drop on $R$ or $L$, so $C$ holds the old source voltage.
**Starting values:** both carry over. The slope is $i/C$.
**Final value:** new DC steady state, $C$ open again, so $v_C\to100\,\mathrm{V}$. Write final value + repeated-root transient.

blocks.answer: $v_C=100+(100+5000t)e^{-50t}\,\mathrm{V}$, $t\ge0$ ($t$ in seconds). It starts at 200 V, flat, and settles at 100 V without overshoot.

blocks.title: Problem 53 · W5 + W6 · The answer is zero · textbook P8.24
blocks.prompt:
The switch has been open a long time; the capacitor is uncharged. At $t=0$ it closes. Find $v_o(t)$ for $t\ge0$.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$12\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$400\,\Omega$"
L1 3,3 -> 3,0 "$1.25\,\mathrm{H}$" i="$i_L$"
S1 3,3 -> 6,3 "$t=0$" action=close
C1 6,3 -> 6,0 "$1.25\,\mu\mathrm{F}$" v="$v_o$"
wire 6,0 -> 0,0
ground 0,0
```

steps.explanation: **Type:** after closing, $L$ and $C$ share the top node, fed through $400\,\Omega$: a parallel RLC with a DC source.
**Before:** $L$ is a short in steady state, so it carries all the source current; $C$ is disconnected and uncharged.
**Starting slope:** at $0^+$, $v_o=0$ so the $400\,\Omega$ still carries $30\,\mathrm{mA}$, and all of it goes into $L$. KCL leaves nothing for $C$.
**Equation:** KCL $\dfrac{v_o-12}{400}+i_L+Cv_o^{\prime}=0$. Differentiating removes the constant 12, so the equation is homogeneous.
**Condition:** a homogeneous linear equation with $v_o(0)=0$ and $v_o^{\prime}(0)=0$ has only the zero solution (the zero-start rule in [Topic C](#topic-c)).

blocks.answer: $v_o(t)=0$ for all $t\ge0$. The inductor already carries the whole source current, so nothing ever flows into the capacitor.
